topic: Operations, Finance and Influences on Business
subject: business-studies

items.title: Small business survival rates are lower than commonly thought
items.claim: ONS UK Business Demography statistics consistently show what 5-year survival rate for new UK businesses?

options.text: Around 40% — roughly six in ten new UK businesses don't survive five years

items.reveal_title: Most new businesses don't make it
items.reveal:
ONS Business Demography data: of UK enterprises born in 2017, 39.6% survived to 2022. Year-1 survival is around 90%; the attrition is concentrated in years 2-5. SME failure causes (UK Federation of Small Businesses surveys) cluster around cash flow, late payment, and lack of management capacity.

Entrepreneurship narratives in business teaching focus on success stories. The base rate is more sobering and is one reason support programmes (start-up loans, mentoring) emphasise survival skills over growth.
items.why: Survivor bias in business case studies hides the failure rate. A textbook with only successful firms gives a misleading picture of what running a business actually involves.

items.title: Profitable businesses fail when cash runs out
items.claim: A construction firm books £5 million revenue and £500,000 profit in 2023 but customers pay 120 days after invoicing while suppliers demand 30 days. What is the most likely outcome?

options.text: Strong cash position because of the reported profit
A cash flow gap large enough to threaten survival, despite profitability — overtrading
Profit and cash will be identical
Suppliers must accept 120-day payment by law

items.reveal:
Carillion, the UK construction giant, reported £147 million profit in 2016 and collapsed in January 2018 with £1.5 billion of debt. A large part of the gap between profit and cash came from long receivable cycles on government contracts combined with aggressive revenue recognition.

'Profit is opinion; cash is fact' is an accounting saying with an empirical basis. The UK Insolvency Service reports that 80%+ of business failures involve a cash-flow rather than profitability problem.
items.why: Reported profit can lead, lag or diverge from cash entirely. Working capital management is often what separates surviving and failing firms.

items.title: Quick ratio strips out the inventory you can't sell fast
items.claim: A retailer has current assets of £600,000 (including £400,000 inventory) and current liabilities of £300,000. What is the quick (acid-test) ratio?
items.reveal:
Quick ratio = (current assets - inventory) / current liabilities = (£600,000 - £400,000) / £300,000 = 0.67. Current ratio would be 2.0 — looking healthy. The acid-test reveals the firm could not cover short-term liabilities without selling stock.

The rule of thumb that quick ratio should exceed 1.0 is industry-dependent. Supermarkets routinely operate below 0.5 because they sell stock for cash before paying suppliers.
items.why: Two firms with identical current ratios can have very different real liquidity. Inventory turnover matters as much as the ratio number.
